title: November 1984
hook: after Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards, mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukamnama: handwritten Granths and the Gurus' letters, gone in a fire. Memory is precious, and today needs that line, because today is about remembering people. Go gently.

On the morning of the thirty-first of October, 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi walked through her garden in New Delhi toward an interview. Two of her own bodyguards, both Sikhs, shot her. She died that day. The news spread through the city in hours. By that evening, and over the next three days, something terrible happened, not to the two men, who were already in custody or dead, but to Sikh families who had nothing to do with it.

From the first of November, mobs moved through parts of Delhi and other cities, hunting Sikhs. They carried lists, or asked neighbors which houses were Sikh. Sikh men and boys were dragged out and killed, many of them burned. Homes, shops and gurdwaras were set on fire. Women were attacked. The worst was in poorer neighborhoods of east and west Delhi, where whole lanes lost their men. For days, the police largely failed to stop it, and in places stood by. Official figures later counted about twenty-seven hundred killed in Delhi alone, and more across India. Many Sikhs believe the true number was higher. Later inquiries and courts found that some local political leaders had led or encouraged the mobs. This was not a riot between two communities. It was violence against one community, for something two men had done. And here the promise from the start of the week holds: no people as a whole are to blame. In those same lanes, there were Hindu families who hid Sikh neighbors in their homes, cut a boy's hair to save his life, or stood at the door and lied to the mob. Their courage is part of the story too. They had names. The people killed were not a number. They were fathers and sons, a shopkeeper, a taxi driver, a teenager coming home. Survivors, many of them widows, have spent their lives making sure the names are said. Remembering someone by name is the smallest and most important thing anyone can do.
screen: `MOBS HUNT SIKH FAMILIES.` · `THOUSANDS KILLED; POLICE STOOD BY.` · `NEIGHBORS WHO HID NEIGHBORS.` · `NOT A NUMBER: PEOPLE.` · then, large: `THEY HAD NAMES.`

segments.voice: For one minute, let your body be still, and say and do nothing. Hold in mind the families of November 1984, the ones who died and the ones who went on living without them; you don't need to picture anything terrible, just keep them company in the quiet. When the minute is over, let the silence stay a little longer.
Yaad. Remembrance — after Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards, mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi, in November 1984. They had names.
Your line: they had names. Each one was someone's person, and someone's loss. Day three hundred ten.

howItsDone: Each November, Sikhs hold remembrance gatherings, Ardas and kirtan for those killed in 1984, and survivors and families read out names and tell their stories.
